stem: Ransomware is actively encrypting files across a file server and spreading to workstations. Which action should the incident responder take first?

options.text: Isolate the affected systems from the network
options.why: Containment comes first. Stopping the spread preserves everything that has not been reached yet.

options.text: Restore the file server from the most recent backup
options.why: Recovery before containment means restoring into an environment that is still actively encrypting, so the restored data is encrypted too.

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan on the file server
options.why: This is eradication, and it is wasted effort while the malware is still reaching new hosts.

options.text: Notify the cyber insurance provider and legal counsel
options.why: Required, and not the first technical action. Notification happens in parallel, it does not stop the spread.

stem: A security incident has been fully remediated and all systems are back in service. Which phase remains?

options.text: Lessons learned
options.why: The final phase captures what happened, what worked, and what changes prevent a repeat. Skipping it means the same incident recurs.

options.text: Containment
options.why: Containment happens during the incident, long before systems return to service.

options.text: Preparation
options.why: Preparation precedes any incident. It is improved by lessons learned, but it is not the phase that follows recovery.

options.text: Detection
options.why: Detection begins the response. Nothing remains to detect for an incident that is closed.

stem: An analyst discovers a workstation communicating with a known command and control server. Legal has confirmed the incident will be pursued. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Disconnect the network cable and leave the system powered on
options.why: Disconnecting contains the host while keeping memory, running processes and network state intact for forensic acquisition.

options.text: Shut the system down immediately to stop the communication
options.why: Shutting down destroys everything in RAM, including the running malware, injected code and open connections. It contains and destroys evidence in one step.

options.text: Leave it connected and continue monitoring indefinitely
options.why: Evidence gathering does not justify letting an active compromise continue once it is confirmed.

options.text: Reimage the workstation and return it to the user
options.why: Reimaging is the eventual remediation and it destroys all evidence. Legal has said the incident will be pursued.

stem: A compromised server is isolated and still running. Which evidence should be collected first?

options.text: A memory image capturing running processes and network connections
options.why: Order of volatility: the most perishable evidence is collected first, and memory disappears the moment power is lost.

options.text: A forensic disk image of the system drive
options.why: Disk is persistent and will still be there after the memory capture. Taking it first risks losing memory to a crash or reboot.

options.text: The SIEM's archived logs for the server
options.why: These are stored elsewhere and are the least volatile evidence in the list.

options.text: Last night's backup tape
options.why: Backups are the most durable evidence of all, and they predate the compromise.

stem: Anticipating litigation, counsel instructs IT to suspend the 90 day email retention policy for six named employees. What is this called?

options.text: A legal hold
options.why: A legal hold suspends routine deletion so potentially relevant data is preserved once litigation is anticipated.

options.text: Chain of custody
options.why: Chain of custody documents who handled evidence already collected. It does not stop a retention policy from deleting data.

options.text: E-discovery
options.why: E-discovery is the later process of identifying and producing the data. The hold is what ensures it still exists to be produced.

options.text: Data sovereignty
options.why: Sovereignty concerns which country's laws govern data based on where it is stored.

stem: A defence attorney argues that a seized hard drive may have been altered between seizure and analysis. Which control answers this challenge?

options.text: A documented chain of custody with hashes taken at each transfer
options.why: It records every person who held the item and when, and the hashes demonstrate the contents did not change.

options.text: A legal hold issued at the time of seizure
options.why: A hold prevents deletion. It says nothing about who handled the drive afterwards.

options.text: Full disk encryption on the seized drive
options.why: Encryption protects confidentiality. It does not evidence integrity of handling.

options.text: An access control list on the evidence storage room
options.why: Useful supporting control, but it does not produce the handling record the challenge demands.

stem: A workstation was compromised by malware that obtained SYSTEM privileges and installed an unknown persistence mechanism. What is the appropriate remediation?

options.text: Reimage from a known good image, then patch and reset the affected credentials
options.why: Once an attacker held full privilege, you cannot enumerate everything they changed. Rebuilding restores a trustworthy state, and the credentials must be reset or they simply return.

options.text: Run the endpoint removal tool and confirm a clean scan
options.why: A clean scan on a host that was fully compromised proves only that the scanner found nothing, which a capable attacker ensures.

options.text: Restore the system from a snapshot taken last week
options.why: The snapshot may predate the compromise or may already contain it, and it restores the unpatched vulnerability either way.

options.text: Remove the malicious service and apply the patch
options.why: This addresses the persistence you found. The scenario says the mechanism is unknown, so you cannot be confident it is the only one.

stem: Ransomware has encrypted a company's file shares. Backups run nightly to a network share mapped on the file server, and those backups are also encrypted. What was the design failure?

options.text: The backups were reachable from the system they protected, so the ransomware reached them too
options.why: Backups must be offline, immutable or otherwise out of reach of a compromised host, or they share its fate.

options.text: Backups were taken too infrequently
options.why: Frequency governs how much data is lost. It would not have helped here, because every copy was encrypted.

options.text: The company did not maintain a ransom payment reserve
options.why: Paying is never the exam's recovery plan, and it does not guarantee a working decryption key.

options.text: The backups were not encrypted at rest
options.why: Encrypting backups protects their confidentiality. It would not have prevented the ransomware from encrypting them again.

stem: After containing a ransomware incident, the organisation holds verified offline backups. What is the correct recovery sequence?

options.text: Rebuild the affected systems, close the vulnerability used, then restore data from the offline backup
options.why: Restoring onto a still vulnerable or still compromised system reinfects it. The hole is closed before data comes back.

options.text: Pay the ransom to obtain the decryption key, since it is faster than restoring
options.why: Payment is not a recovery control. It may be unlawful, it funds further attacks, and the key may not work.

options.text: Restore the data immediately to minimise downtime, then patch
options.why: This restores into a compromised environment, which is how organisations get encrypted a second time during recovery.

options.text: Decrypt in place with a public decryptor and leave the systems running
options.why: Even where a decryptor exists, the systems remain compromised and untrustworthy.

stem: Which pair of actions correctly matches the incident response phase they belong to?

options.text: Isolating an infected host is containment; removing the malware is eradication
options.why: Containment limits the damage while it is happening. Eradication removes the cause afterwards.

options.text: Isolating an infected host is eradication; patching is containment
options.why: Both are reversed. Isolation stops spread, patching closes the underlying weakness.

options.text: Restoring from backup is containment; isolating is recovery
options.why: Restoring is recovery and isolating is containment. This inverts them.

options.text: Writing the incident report is eradication; the post-incident meeting is recovery
options.why: Both belong to lessons learned, which follows recovery.

stem: Rank these sources from most to least volatile: disk, remote logging server, RAM, CPU cache.

options.text: CPU cache, RAM, disk, remote logging server
options.why: Volatility decreases in that order, and it is the order in which evidence should be collected.

options.text: RAM, CPU cache, disk, remote logging server
options.why: CPU registers and cache are more volatile than RAM, surviving only nanoseconds.

options.text: Disk, RAM, CPU cache, remote logging server
options.why: This begins with one of the most persistent sources, which is the classic inversion.

options.text: Remote logging server, disk, RAM, CPU cache
options.why: This is exactly reversed. Off-host logs are the most durable of the four.

stem: A responder must contain a compromised laptop while preserving evidence. Which action achieves both?

options.text: Disable its switch port or move it to a quarantine VLAN, leaving it powered on
options.why: The host is cut off from the network while memory, processes and connections stay intact for acquisition.

options.text: Perform a graceful shutdown so no data is corrupted
options.why: A graceful shutdown is gentler on the file system and just as fatal to volatile evidence, and it may trigger anti-forensic cleanup.

options.text: Pull the power cable to prevent any further writes
options.why: This preserves disk state at the cost of every byte of memory evidence.

options.text: Run a full antivirus removal before anything else
options.why: Eradication before containment and before acquisition destroys the evidence and does not stop the spread.

stem: An analyst reads a report on a group that abuses a specific signed binary for persistence, then searches twelve months of endpoint telemetry for that pattern across the estate. No alert prompted this. What activity is it?

options.text: Threat hunting
options.why: A hypothesis drawn from intelligence, investigated deliberately, with no alert involved. The point is to find what no existing rule would have caught.

options.text: Detection
options.why: Detection is rule, signature or baseline driven and begins when something fires. Nothing fired here.

options.text: Analysis, as an incident response phase
options.why: Analysis establishes scope and nature of a known incident. There is no incident yet.

options.text: A vulnerability scan
options.why: A scan enumerates weaknesses that exist. This searches for evidence that someone has already acted.

stem: A threat hunt finds no compromise but reveals that a particular administrative technique would have gone entirely unlogged. What is the most valuable outcome?

options.text: Create the logging and detection rule, converting the gap into something monitoring will catch in future
options.why: A hunt that finds nothing is not a wasted hunt. Its usual product is a new detection, which is how hunting feeds back into monitoring.

options.text: Conclude the environment is clean and close the hunt
options.why: Finding nothing is weak evidence of absence and leaves the blind spot exactly where it was.

options.text: Open an incident so the gap is formally tracked
options.why: No incident occurred. This is a control gap, handled through remediation rather than incident response.

options.text: Schedule a penetration test to confirm the gap
options.why: The gap is already confirmed. Paying to rediscover it delays the fix.

stem: After containment, a team restores forty workstations from backup and returns them to the network. Within two days the same malware reappears on several of them. What was most likely skipped?

options.text: Eradication: the cause was never fully removed, so recovery restored systems into an environment that still held it
options.why: Recovery follows eradication for this exact reason. Restoring while the root cause persists reproduces the incident, which is the single most common sequencing error.

options.text: Recovery was performed incorrectly from the wrong backup set
options.why: Possible, and the pattern of several hosts reinfecting after return points to something still live in the environment.

options.text: Lessons learned, which should precede recovery
options.why: Lessons learned is the final phase. It would not have prevented this.

options.text: Reporting to the regulator
options.why: An obligation that may well exist and has no bearing on reinfection.

stem: A breach involving personal data is confirmed on a Friday morning. The investigation will take at least three weeks. Legal asks about notification. What governs the timing?

options.text: Statutory deadlines generally run from becoming aware of the breach, not from completing the investigation, so notification cannot wait for the full picture
options.why: Regimes commonly require notification within a short window, often 72 hours, with details supplemented later. Waiting for certainty is how organisations miss it.

options.text: Notification is due once root cause analysis is complete
options.why: That would let the clock depend on the investigation's length, which is why no regime defines it that way.

options.text: Notification is only required if the data is confirmed to have been misused
options.why: The trigger is usually unauthorised access or disclosure, not evidence of downstream harm.

options.text: There is no obligation while the incident remains contained internally
options.why: Containment governs the technical response. It does not discharge a notification duty.

stem: An organisation gathers its response team and legal counsel around a table to talk through a ransomware scenario, deciding who would do what. No systems are touched. Which preparation activity is this?

options.text: A tabletop exercise
options.why: Discussion-based, no tooling, focused on decisions, roles and gaps in the plan. It is the cheapest exercise and often the most revealing about who is unclear on their role.

options.text: A simulation
options.why: A simulation uses real tooling against an injected scenario. The stem says nothing is touched.

options.text: A failover test
options.why: That actually moves production to the secondary site.

options.text: Threat hunting
options.why: Hunting searches live telemetry for evidence of an actual intruder.

stem: Why does an incident response plan require training and exercises rather than only a written document?

options.text: Under pressure people execute what they have practised; an untested plan surfaces its gaps during the incident
options.why: Preparation is the first phase for this reason. Exercises find the missing contact, the unclear authority and the assumption nobody checked, while it is still cheap to find them.

options.text: Regulations require a specific number of exercises per year
options.why: Some regimes do set expectations, and the reason the activity exists is competence rather than compliance.

options.text: Exercises replace the need for a documented plan
options.why: They validate the plan. Without the document there is nothing to exercise against.

options.text: They provide the evidence needed for chain of custody
options.why: Chain of custody documents handling of evidence during a real incident.

stem: Containment and eradication are complete after a confirmed intrusion. Which TWO activities remain outstanding as named incident response activities? (Choose two.)

options.text: Recovery: returning systems to normal service and confirming they are clean and functioning
options.why: Recovery follows eradication and is a distinct phase, including validation that service is genuinely restored.

options.text: Lessons learned: changing what allowed the incident so it is not repeated
options.why: The final phase, routinely skipped, and the only one that improves the odds next time.

options.text: Detection, since monitoring must be re-enabled
options.why: Detection precedes analysis and containment. It is not a closing activity.

options.text: Preparation, since the plan must be written
options.why: Preparation happens before any incident. Improvements to it arrive through lessons learned.

options.text: Threat hunting, which is the final phase of incident response
options.why: Hunting is a proactive activity, not a phase in the response to a known incident.

stem: A worm is spreading and legal has asked for a full forensic investigation. Which TWO actions belong to containment and preserve evidence? (Choose two.)

options.text: Disconnect the affected hosts from the network, leaving them powered on
options.why: Stops the spread while memory, processes and connections survive for acquisition.

options.text: Block the worm's port between workstation subnets at the switch
options.why: Network segmentation stops lateral movement across every host at once, and touches no evidence.

options.text: Power off every affected host immediately
options.why: Contains the spread and destroys every byte of volatile evidence, which legal has just asked for.

options.text: Reimage the affected hosts from a known good image
options.why: Reimaging is eradication, it comes later, and it destroys the evidence.

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan on every workstation
options.why: Scanning is eradication one host at a time while the worm keeps reinfecting from neighbours.
